title: Prospective multimodal phenotyping of mild arm and hand motor deficits after stroke
summary:
After a stroke or a temporary disturbance of blood flow to the brain, mild problems with arm and hand movements may remain. These problems are not always fully detected during a routine examination, but they may still affect everyday activities.

The aim of this study is to describe such mild movement problems in more detail. The study will examine whether typical movement patterns can be identified by combining different types of assessments and how these patterns are related to the difficulties reported by the participants and to changes seen in brain imaging.

Adults who have had a stroke or a temporary disturbance of blood flow to the brain within the previous 14 days may take part. Arm and hand strength and movement will be examined. Participants will also perform standardized movement tasks that are recorded on video and complete tasks on a tablet. They will answer questions about their symptoms and limitations in daily life. Results from routine clinical examinations and existing brain scans will also be evaluated. An additional voluntary follow-up assessment may take place after approximately 90 days.

interventions.name: Ischemic stroke / transient ischemic attack (TIA), with a focus on newly occurring mild to moderate arm/hand impairments of the upper extremity; comparison with patients without clinically detectable motor impairment of the upper extremity.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Capacity to provide informed consent.

2. Age ≥ 18 years.

3. Clinical diagnosis of ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA).

4. Presence of either
   a) newly occurring mild to moderate arm/hand impairment in the context of the current event, defined as a motor deficit of the upper extremity on admission examination (NIHSS Motor Arm score 0–2) and/or a subjectively reported new impairment of the arm/hand (e.g., fine motor skills, strength, coordination),
   or
   b) no motor impairment of the upper extremity.

5. Symptom onset ≤ 14 days before study enrollment.

6. Sufficient ability to cooperate in order to complete the video assessments, e.g., adequate language comprehension and no aphasia, neglect, apraxia, or cognitive impairment that would prevent valid performance of the tasks.

7. Willingness to undergo standardized video recording of upper-extremity motor tasks and to allow scientific analysis of the resulting movement features in accordance with the informed consent, including pseudonymized analysis of standardized video recordings for the derivation of quantitative movement features.
Exclusion criteria:
1. Lack of capacity to provide informed consent or inability to provide comprehensive information/obtain informed consent.

2. Insufficient ability to cooperate, such that the video-/tablet-based tasks cannot be performed validly, e.g., severe aphasia with lack of instruction comprehension, pronounced neglect, severe apraxia, significant cognitive impairment/delirium.

3. Pre-existing relevant arm/hand functional impairment of the upper extremity, e.g., previous hemiparesis, severe osteoarthritis, relevant contractures, known peripheral nerve lesion, or amputation-/prosthesis-related limitation, which would substantially confound attribution to the current event or interpretation of the measurements.

4. Acute non-neurological impairment of the upper extremity that substantially limits performance or interpretation, e.g., fracture, severe pain, acute inflammation/immobilization.

5. Pronounced movement disorders that dominate the measurement and complicate interpretation with regard to paresis, e.g., severe tremor or severe dyskinesia.

6. Severe systemic disease/clinical instability that precludes participation for safety or organizational reasons.
